1.pericope_label: Midian and the seven years of oppression

schools.summary: Gill dates the relapse to the deaths of Deborah and Barak, who had held the nation to pure worship while they lived, and describes the raiders' calendar: they left Israel alone through winter and seedtime so that the ground was manured and sown, and came only when there was a crop to take.

Henry finds the scourge humiliating in itself. Israel had smarted often enough, yet like a burnt child returning to the fire went back to idolatry with a revolting rebellious heart, and the instrument God used was despicable — no king, lord or general on the Midianite side, but an undisciplined mob drawn from a nation Israel had all but destroyed two centuries before, so that God moved his people to jealousy by those who were not a people. He blames the flight to the caves on their own guilty consciences, since sin dispirits men, and sees exact justice in the loss of a harvest they had withheld from God in tithes and prepared for Baal instead.

Clarke identifies Midian as among the most ancient and inveterate of Israel's enemies, places them on the eastern shore of the Dead Sea with Arnon for their capital, recalls that they had once been all but wiped out, and describes the raiders arriving early to watch the ripening fields until, driven from the plain, the Israelites lived like wild beasts and were hunted like them.

Ellicott traces Midian to Abraham by Keturah and remembers the Baal-peor affair that made the hostility deadly; he explains the raiders' economics — living by idleness and plunder, they let others grow the corn and came to reap it — and finds the same in Alyattes of Lydia, who leaves the houses of Miletus standing so their owners will plough again, and among the Fellahîn of his own century, who sow in dread of the Bedouin and keep huge underground hiding-places. He prefers locusts to grasshoppers, notes that the Bedouin call locusts the host of God, remarks that camels were very uncommon in Palestine, and treats the numbers as oriental hyperbole, quoting Burckhardt's Bedouin who threw up a handful of sand. Keil and Delitzsch reconstruct the route over the Jordan near Beisan, through Jezreel and westward to Gaza, and read the definite article in the dens and caves as showing these were known refuges still standing when the book was written, the verb covering the use of a natural cavern as well as the digging of one.

debates: Whether Israel dug the hiding-places or used existing caverns. Keil and Delitzsch hold that the statement that Israel made them does not exclude the natural caverns of the limestone hills, since the verb covers using a cave as well as excavating one.

7.pericope_label: The prophet sent before the deliverer

schools.summary: Gill drives a wedge between the cry and its cause: Israel cried under Midianite oppression, not under the sins that had brought it, of which they seemed to have no sense — and God, meaning to deliver them, sent a messenger first to give them that sense. He rejects the Jewish identification of the prophet with Phinehas on chronology, since Phinehas could hardly have lived more than two centuries and nothing was heard of him under the preceding judges, and adds the deliverance at the sea to the recital of favours.

Henry finds encouragement in the cry being heard at all, from a people who had neglected God in prosperity and turned to him only under extremity, and reads the order of God's acts as a promise: a prophet before an angel, conviction before rescue, so that their crying might carry confession. Furnishing a land with faithful ministers is itself a token for good. He calls the required obedience easy and equitable — fear God and you need not fear the gods of the Amorites — and makes the single clause of indictment the hinge, since disobedience to God is the malignity of all sin, and repentance is genuine only when that, rather than the trouble sin brings, is chiefly lamented.
Clarke reports the Phinehas tradition but prefers some teacher raised up for the purpose, one of the witnesses God sent from time to time to declare his counsel.

Ellicott notes how freely the Hagadah supplies names for anonymous prophets — Iddo for the man at Bethel, Jonah for the young man who anointed Jehu — stresses that the Hebrew says a man, a prophet, and not an angel as in the earlier chapter, guesses the audience may have been a feast-day assembly, identifies the Amorites as the highlanders of Palestine and the most powerful of the Canaanite tribes, and states the principle the chapter turns on: no deliverance is promised until repentance has begun. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same intention as a sequence, reproof before help, so that the people might recognise their misery as chastisement for apostasy and repent by remembering what grace had formerly done.

debates: Who the prophet was. Jewish legend names Phinehas son of Eleazar; Ellicott reports it as an instance of the Hagadah's habit of naming anonymous prophets, Clarke prefers an unnamed teacher raised up for the occasion, and Gill rejects the identification outright on chronological grounds.

schools.summary: Gill identifies the visitor as no created angel but the Angel of Jehovah's presence, the Word and Son of God, who is expressly called Jehovah in the passage.

Henry agrees, adding on bishop Patrick's authority that these appearances in human shape were a prelude to the incarnation, when God would take our nature for good and all; and he reads the circumstances of the meeting as three lessons. Gideon was alone, and God often manifests himself out of the noise and hurry of the world; he was employed, beating out wheat with a rod, a man of account with servants who still would not live in idleness, so that honest business put him in the way of a divine visit as keeping their flocks did the shepherds; and he was distressed, hiding by the winepress, the day of greatest distress being God's time to appear. From threshing corn, Henry says, he is fetched to thresh the Midianites. He also notes that Joash was alive but passed over for keeping up Baal's worship, and that the judges had hitherto been raised out of the tribe that suffered most.

Clarke explains the oddity of the site: a threshing-floor could not be used in open day for fear of the Midianites, who carried off the grain as soon as it was beaten out, so Gideon fetched a few sheaves to be threshed privately, and since the distress meant there was no vintage a winepress was the last place raiders would look for corn. He places Ophrah in the half tribe beyond Jordan, and finds the summons from farm work unremarkable in one way and instructive in another, citing Shamgar the ploughman and Cincinnatus fetched from the plough to be dictator of Rome.

Ellicott calls the suggestion of a prophet obviously absurd, the word there being nabi and here the messenger of Jehovah, and dismisses Josephus's phantasm in the shape of a youth as his usual dressing of the story for Gentile readers. He prefers terebinth to oak, puts Ophrah in western Manasseh and follows Van de Velde in identifying it with Erfai, gives the meanings of the names — Ophrah a fawn, Gideon a hewer — prefers beating out to threshing since a winepress was a vat sunk in the ground, renders the phrase for hiding it literally as making it fly, and observes that the open circular threshing-floors would be an invader's first target. Keil and Delitzsch describe the guise chosen, a traveller with a staff, point out that the town and not the tree belonged to Joash, identify Abiezer as a small family in Manasseh of which he was probably head, and decline to locate Ophrah at all.

debates: Where Ophrah stood. Ellicott places it in western Manasseh and identifies it with Erfai near the northern border of Ephraim; Clarke puts it in the half tribe beyond Jordan; Keil and Delitzsch decline to settle the question.
outliers: Clarke's parallel for the call is not scriptural but Roman: Cincinnatus fetched from the plough to be dictator, a case he thinks strikingly like Gideon's.

schools.summary: Gill marks the moment the visitor stops waiting under the oak and comes forward to stand in Gideon's sight, and takes the title Gideon used in reply to show that he thought him no angel but some illustrious and eminent person.

Clarke prefers the Targum's reverent form of the greeting, the Word of the Lord is with thee, infers from the title that Gideon had already given proof of courage and personal prowess, and turns the observation into a rule about calling: God picks instruments whom his workings in nature and providence have already fitted for the purpose, and though they look unlikely they prove the best qualified. Of the reply he says only that it is remarkable for energy and simplicity, and that the despondency in it goes no further than the case warranted.

Ellicott counts the greeting out as three Hebrew words and notes that it was once an ordinary salutation and blessing; he doubts the title can refer merely to the energy of the flail, and gathers the scattered glimpses of Gideon's unnarrated years — a possible fight on Mount Tabor or even in the Canaanite war, a kingly presence, a youthful son, many slaves, an armour-bearer. He makes the address in reply a bare courtesy, adoni, and hears in the phrase all this an echo of Gideon's own brooding, quoting the bitter turn Josephus gives it. Keil and Delitzsch read the whole greeting as promise rather than compliment, pledging that by the Lord's strength Gideon would prove the hero he was called, and describe the answer as doubting rather than defiant, recalling the sentence of Deuteronomy and supposing that Gideon had been turning over his nation's misery at his work without seeing any possibility of rescue.

Gill has Jehovah himself — the same person just called his angel — gaze earnestly at Gideon and smile on him, showing that he bore him kindness and meant him well, and quotes the Targum on the promise that follows: my Word shall be thy help, which he thinks answers every plea of meanness, unworthiness and weakness at once.

Clarke supplies the arithmetic behind the word family, tribes having been divided anciently into tens, fifties, hundreds and thousands, so that a thousand marked a grand division and a numerous kindred; Gideon means either that his own has dwindled or, if the word is a shortened plural, that the thousands in Manasseh are thinned. On the promise he offers both readings, that Gideon should overcome the whole host as surely as if he had one man to fight, or else destroy them to a man.

Ellicott notes that the speaker now talks as the Lord, as in the visit to Abraham, and reports the inference that this is the angel of the covenant, the captain of the Lord's host, the only alternative being to treat him as the mouth of God; he takes the looking literally though it carries favour with it, says the look put fresh force into the man, and explains that the Greek translators keep the angel of the Lord throughout out of Alexandrian distaste for anthropomorphism. He renders the adjective in Gideon's plea the meanest rather than poor, compares David called the little one among his brethren, notes that Gideon was the last of his father's house as well as the least since his brothers had been killed, and finds such diffidence regularly in men God chooses. Keil and Delitzsch account for the change of name in the narrative by the reply itself, which echoes the commissioning of Moses, gloss this thy strength as the strength conferred by the promise just made, and read the smiting of Midian as one man to mean at a single blow.

debates: Whether Gideon at this point says adoni or Adonai. Ellicott notes that our translators deliberately read the courteous form, on the ground that Gideon did not fully recognise his visitor until the disappearance, whereas the Hebrew manuscripts read Adonai, Lord — the reading Keil and Delitzsch adopt, taking Gideon to have perceived already that he was not dealing with a man.

17.pericope_label: The sign asked for and the offering fetched

schools.summary: Gill notes that the grace Gideon pleads is grace he has evidently found already, in the salutation that called him a man of might, in the charge laid on him and in the pledge of success; and takes the errand at face value, a run to his father's house for food to entertain the visitor with.

Clarke wants an outright miracle, one that would satisfy Gideon that his visitor had wisdom and power enough to authorise and qualify him for the task; and he keeps the hospitable side of the offering, noting that a minchah was commonly bread, wine, oil and flour, and that although the request suggests Gideon took the stranger for a divine person, what he actually prepared looks like refreshment for a guest of consequence.

Ellicott observes that the phrase about finding grace runs through both Testaments and paraphrases the request as asking clear proof that this is no mere vision and that the message means him well; on the offering he points out that minchah means an offering, and above all an offering to God, which is why the Greek turns the clause into a promise to sacrifice, yet thinks the neutral word deliberately chosen by a man who suspected without yet being persuaded, with plain hospitality mixed into his growing awe. Keil and Delitzsch hold that after the promise Gideon could no longer doubt that the words came in God's name, so that the sign is asked for something narrower — assurance that the speaker was himself God — and note that the Hebrew turn of phrase is borrowed from everyday conversation; they weigh the minchah as no sacrifice in the technical sense and no present of food either, but a gift laid before God on whose acceptance the sign would turn.

debates: What Gideon meant by his minchah. Keil and Delitzsch make it a sacrificial gift laid before God, on whose acceptance the sign depended; Ellicott agrees the word means an offering to God but thinks Gideon chose a neutral term on purpose; Clarke reads what was actually prepared as a meal for a respected traveller.

schools.summary: Gill marks the refusal of the meal — rather than sit down to what had been prepared, the visitor issued instructions — and remarks that the staff was the one he had been walking with, part of why Gideon pressed food on him before he should go on his way.

Clarke matches the entertainment against living custom, citing Dr Shaw's account of an Arab host — milk, figs, raisins or dates to stay the guest's appetite, then a kid or lamb from the flock, half seethed at once and served with cucasoe and the rest roasted as kab-ab for the next day — and follows Harmer in reading the verse the same way, with the roasted portion packed for the traveller's road and the meal carried out to a tent whose shade and the oak's together kept off the sun. He states the purpose of the instructions plainly, the flesh and bread to become an offering and the broth a libation, describes the touch and the fire rising out of the rock as the most evident proof of supernatural agency, and adds that the disappearance ended nothing, God continuing to speak with Gideon by secret impression or audible voice.

Ellicott explains the unleavened cakes as the quickest bread to make, reckons the ephah at about twenty-two and a half pounds where a homer would have sufficed — Eastern hospitality holding nothing too lavish — and splits the difference between the Greek manuscripts on the verb for presenting, approached being too weak and worshipped too strong. He notices that the speaker is here alone in the chapter the angel of Elohim, renders the direction as pointing to yonder crag, gathers parallels for the pouring from Genesis, from Elijah's sea-water and from the thick water called Naphthai that Nehemiah poured out, calls the staff the ordinary equipment of an Eastern traveller, sets the flame among its fellows as the usual token of God's acceptance, and draws the contrast that water comes out of the rock for man's blessing and fire to show that God is there. Keil and Delitzsch say simply that in the miracle Gideon received the sign he had asked for.

outliers: Ellicott notes what the text does not say — that the angel ascended in the flame, as happens in the later chapter.

schools.summary: Gill has Gideon work out who his visitor was from the miracle and the manner of the departure, offers a secret impulse on his spirit or a voice out of heaven for the reassurance, and cites Kimchi's suggestion that the angel, having ascended and seeing the man's terror, caused the voice to be heard — which he treats as further proof that this angel was Jehovah, the eternal Word. He puts the altar on the crown of the rock where the food had lain, the fire having certified acceptance and promised that Midian would be consumed as quickly.

Clarke calls the cry elliptical, the natural speech of a distressed mind, and supplies what is missing; he reports the belief that whoever saw God or his representative angel must die as settled before the law and under it, and finds it among the heathen too in the fable of Jupiter and Semele and in the hymn of Callimachus. He draws the moral that the discovery was God's own doing and not the fruit of prying into forbidden mysteries, translates the altar's name as the Lord is my peace or the peace of Jehovah, and reads the words behind it as prediction and not merely good wish.

Ellicott says the last sign gave Gideon a far deeper sense of his visitor's grandeur, holds that nothing need be supplied in the broken cry though the alarm shows what the fear was, corrects the rendering to for to this end, calls the belief universal among the Jews and adds Actæon and Psyche to Semele. He admits the text does not say how the reassurance came and notes that the Greek translators here leave the Lord standing; on the altar he cites the altar Ed, raised by the tribes across Jordan, as an instance of altars built to commemorate rather than to burn anything, and closes with the company the name keeps in Jehovah-jireh, Jehovah-nissi and Jehovah-tsidkenu. Keil and Delitzsch classify the exclamation as one Hebrew uses for dread of an expected calamity, are certain the words of peace were God's and not the angel's parting speech, and insist the altar was no place of sacrifice but a memorial and witness, standing until the book was written, that the Lord meant peace and not wrath toward Israel.

debates: Whether the Jehovah-shalom altar was a memorial only. Keil and Delitzsch insist it was never a place of sacrifice, and Ellicott cites commemorative altars as the parallel; Clarke suggests it is the very altar mentioned a little later, named here by anticipation, which would make it a place of sacrifice after all.

schools.summary: Gill dates the second word to the night after the day of the threshing-floor.

Henry treats the dream as the correspondence kept up by another route, God speaking while Gideon was still full of what had passed and had told nobody, with the encouragement that God's visits, gratefully received, are graciously repeated. The new judge begins his government at home; grace raised both a reformer and a rescuer out of the household of a ringleader in idolatry; and keeping away from the altar was not enough, since God commands the monuments of superstition down before he enjoins his own service — not, as bishop Hall notes, re-consecrating them. He finds two purposes in the order, to test the man's zeal before the field tested his courage and to begin the reformation, sin being the cause and oppression its effect; cites bishop Patrick for taking the grove to mean the image in it; and allots the two beasts, the young bullock for Gideon and the older for the sins of the people, peace being made with God before war on Midian.

Clarke guesses the second bullock had been fattened for Baal, being so carefully distinguished from one of Joash's, and reasons that since the altar stood on Joash's land yet seems to have been common property, the beast was likely reared at the villagers' charge — or why should they resent its going to Jehovah?

Ellicott, following Luther, warns against picturing a voice in the air and thinks it useless to ask how the intimation came; what it made plain was that Gideon must be an iconoclast before he could be a deliverer. He insists on naming the Asherah rather than a grove, notes that it stood on the altar and not beside it and that no image of Baal is mentioned at all, and states the principle that God being one and jealous of the easy blending of idolatries, Baal's altar must come down before God's goes up. On the conjunction he prefers and to Ewald's even, since two beasts' labour would not be too much and a seven-year-old would hardly be called a young bullock; he reports the Chaldee's fattened seven years, perhaps glancing at the oppression, observes that no age for burnt offerings was fixed by law, and takes the unexplained minuteness of the detail as evidence that the narrative is no legend, conjecturing that the first beast was Joash's and meant for Baal and the second Gideon's own votive animal, kept fattening against the longed-for day. Keil and Delitzsch give the reason for the command — Israel could not be freed until his father's house was purged and his own life sanctified by a burnt offering — and note that the first bullock is never heard of again, which has driven most commentators to suppose both were offered.

debates: What the two bullocks were for. Keil and Delitzsch report that most commentators suppose both were sacrificed, since the first is never mentioned again; Clarke takes the second to have been fattened for Baal at the villagers' charge; Ellicott conjectures the first was Joash's, meant for Baal, and the second Gideon's own votive beast; Henry divides them between Gideon himself and the people he was to rescue.

26.pericope_label: The altar built and the command obeyed by night

schools.summary: Gill puts the new altar on the crown of the rock beside the memorial already standing there, and holds that these were two altars and not one — the earlier a monument meant to last, this one for sacrifice and for the occasion only, the tabernacle being the proper place for offerings. On the disputed phrase he offers two senses, the spot where Gideon had been told to lay the flesh and cakes or else the orderly fashion the law required, an altar of earth and unhewn stone. He explains the ten servants both ways, men Gideon could order and also men he could trust, who like himself had never bowed the knee, the night's work needing hands enough for dispatch.

Clarke takes the Asherah for Astarte and supposes a wooden image of the goddess standing on Baal's altar, the pair well matched, Baal-peor answering to Priapus and Astarte to Venus; wood, he adds, is what early and rude peoples make their gods of and still do, instancing the islanders of the South Sea, the Indians of America, the people of Ceylon whose images of Budhoo are largely wooden, and the Scandinavians. From the fear he infers that Joash was an idolater, and from the trusted servants that Gideon had kept the true faith.

Ellicott finds the word for rock here to be neither of the two used a few verses back but maoz, a stronghold, probably the citadel of Ophrah, a word belonging elsewhere only to poetry; he doubts both text and margin on the ordered place, reports that some translate with the materials and that the Jews were plainly unsure themselves, and takes it to mean with the Asherah pillar hewn down and split into firewood. He lists the four irregularities the Jews counted against the offering — not at Shiloh, not by a priest, by night, and kindled with the timber of an idol — and argues that God's command more than covered them, the Levitic order having become impossible at many points with the country in heathen hands. He reads the ten servants as evidence of Gideon's standing and of an effort to keep his household clean amid an almost universal defection, glosses the father's house as the Abi-ezrites, and remarks that many of the townsmen may have been Canaanite by race. Keil and Delitzsch fix the timing and the motive together, the work done with those ten men in the night, and no doubt the very night the word came, because doing it by day meant facing his family and the town.

Gill has the townsmen out early at the place of the altar, the grove and the image, come to pay their morning devotions, describes them amazed and unable to imagine who would dare anything so wicked, and then has the chief inhabitants meet and go in a body to Joash, their chief magistrate, to have justice done.

Clarke ties the choice of victim to its age — seven years old, calved about the time the oppression began, and killed now to signify that the servitude would expire with its life, the younger beast serving as a peace-offering and the older as the burnt offering. He thinks the townsmen fastened on Gideon the sooner because they knew he had never joined their worship, and explains their heat by their interest: every man had a stake in rites that afforded him a good deal of sensual gratification, which is why Baal and Ashtaroth would always draw more worshippers than the true God.

Ellicott notes that Eastern habits are early anyway and that Baal-worship may well have included some greeting of the rising sun, and counts the three things that met them — the wrecked altar, the stump of the felled Asherah, and a new altar with a burnt offering smoking on it. He doubts the alternative that Gideon offered both bullocks, since the text says nothing of what became of the young one and Gideon might have hesitated to give the Lord an animal perhaps vowed to Baal; he observes that we are not told the servants gave their master away, since suspicion would naturally settle on so conspicuous a worshipper of Jehovah and work needing that many hands is seldom kept quiet, and that Gideon had proved himself what his name means. He finds it hard to conceive that these townsmen were Israelites at all. Keil and Delitzsch add the practical reason the evidence survived — the bullock would not have burned away entirely — and pause on the passive construction taking an accusative and on the ambiguity of who answered the question.

debates: Whether both bullocks were sacrificed. Clarke assigns the young beast a peace-offering and the seven-year-old the burnt offering; Ellicott reports the same division as a supposition and doubts it, since nothing is said of the young bullock's fate.

schools.summary: Gill takes those Joash addresses to be his son's accusers, pressing for the young man to be handed over and killed.

Clarke marks the emphasis in the challenge and points to the lengthened verb forms that thicken it — will you plead in earnest, will you really rescue him. Joash could not kill his son and was satisfied the insult to Baal was real; if Baal were truly God he would right his own honour. The heathen thought so too, and Clarke produces Tacitus, who has Tiberius write that heaven was not decreed to Augustus in order to trap citizens, that an image sold with houses and grounds is no wrong to religion, and that injuries done to the gods are the gods' own business; and Livy, who reports senators pretending that a disputed matter concerned the gods rather than themselves and that the gods would see their rites were not polluted.

Ellicott finds the phrase for those addressed genuinely obscure and thinks it may mean no more than the bystanders; he calls the speech extraordinarily bold and cunning, suspects the son's courage had stirred the father's conscience, and shows how Joash saves him — not by defending the act but by counterfeiting a zeal so hot that doubting Baal's power to avenge himself becomes the blasphemy, so that Baal-worship is turned into the argument for leaving Baal's injury unavenged. Time was the point: he reads the Hebrew, with the Greek, the Vulgate, the Syriac, the Arabic and the Chaldee, as before to-morrow's sun rises, remarks that in a popular tumult delay is safety, and observes that among idolaters an act of open contempt that draws no thunder shakes the worshippers' reverence — instancing the sneers of Aristophanes, Persius and Lucían at a Jupiter who cannot defend his own temple, Olaf's destruction of the image of Odin, and the priest Coifi riding at the Saxon idols in armour and on horseback. Keil and Delitzsch mark the doubled pronoun as emphatic, resist the reading that makes till the morning mean a summary execution before daybreak, and attach the words elsewhere in the sentence; they also read the name that came of the day, Jerubbaal, as let Baal contend, a taunt that soon became a title of honour once it was plain Baal could do the man no harm, and note its later form Jerubbesheth, Bosheth being a nickname for Baal as in Ishbosheth for Eshbaal.

debates: What till the morning attaches to. Keil and Delitzsch reject Bertheau's sense of a summary execution before daybreak, holding that the words will not bear it and belong elsewhere in the clause; Ellicott, with the ancient versions, reads them as a proposal to wait and see whether Baal will avenge himself.

schools.summary: Gill has Joash give his son the title, and reports the identification of Jerubbaal with Jerombalus, priest of the god Jevo, from whom the ancient Phoenician writer Sanchoniatho is said, on Philo Byblius's authority, to have drawn the substance of what he wrote about the Jews.

Clarke renders the name let Baal contend and translates the substitution a later book makes, bosheth — confusion or ignominy — put in place of baal, lord, so that the man now contends against shame. On Sanchoniatho he is blunt: the history is probably Porphyry's own forgery and worth no credit whatever.

Ellicott makes the naming impersonal, so that Gideon got the name rather than his father conferred it, allows the senses let it be striven with Baal or Baal's antagonist as helping the name catch on, and wonders whether the Palmyrene deity Jaribolos lies behind it. He explains the later disfigurement as the Jews' literal reading of the law against naming other gods, which is how Esh-baal and Merib-baal reach us as Ishbosheth and Mephibosheth and what the ancients meant by charging the nation with contumelia numinum, but enters Ewald's caution that both words may once have carried less offensive associations, there having been a Baal among Saul's own ancestors. He notes the Greek spelling Hierobalos and quotes Eusebius, from the same Philo, for Sanchoniatho of Berytus being helped by Hierombalos, priest of the god Iao.

debates: Whether Gideon is the Hierombalos of Sanchoniatho. Gill and Ellicott report the identification with interest, Ellicott adding that Eusebius praises Sanchoniatho's accuracy in Jewish matters; Clarke dismisses the whole history as a forgery of Porphyry's.

schools.summary: Gill denies that the invasion was retaliation: this was the raiders' usual season for crossing into Canaan, harvest time, as Gideon's threshing shows, and they came as they had for years to carry off the increase of the earth.

Henry allows that they may have come to plead for Baal and make his altar a pretext, but prefers the annual explanation and notes that they were expected while Gideon was at the winepress, God having raised the deliverer up in time. Nobody cared or dared to hold so important a pass; their headquarters lay in the heart of Manasseh, near Gideon's own town; and long success with feeble opposition had made them confident — but the measure of their iniquity was full, and men who had spoiled so long must now be spoiled, gathered like sheaves to the floor for Gideon to thresh. He finds the muster remarkable twice over, in the men of Abiezer who had lately demanded his life and now took him for their commander, so suddenly can God turn the hearts of idolaters and persecutors, and in tribes as far off as Asher and Naphtali who reckoned that if their neighbours were overrun their own turn came next. On the signs he is gentle: perhaps Gideon wanted them for his followers rather than himself, and at bottom the request means Lord, I believe, help thou my unbelief. The apology before the second sign Henry sets beside Abraham's, and finds in the whole business how tender God is of weak believers, that the bruised reed be not broken; the reversal answered the objection that wool naturally takes up moisture, and Dr Fuller's remark on it is that heaven's real miracles will endure turning, being inside and outside both alike. Could God tell a small fleece of Israel from the vast floor of Midian? He could — and in one congregation one soul is the moistened fleece, another the dry ground.
Clarke thinks the raiders heard what Gideon had done, took it for a first bid for liberty, and formed a general league against Israel.

Ellicott agrees it was the annual raid and adds that thousands besides Gideon had been reaping and threshing in secret as soon as the wheat was ripe; taking the fords by Bethshean, he would put the camp not in the broad plain but in the trough between Gilboa and Little Hermon, and notes the meaning of the name, God's sowing. Keil and Delitzsch have them cross the Jordan near Beisan and pitch in the valley of Jezreel.

debates: Why Midian came when it did. Clarke reads the invasion as a response to the destruction of Baal's altar; Gill denies any connection and makes it the ordinary harvest raid; Ellicott agrees with Gill, and Henry allows Clarke's explanation as possible but prefers the other.
outliers: Henry passes on Dr Fuller's remark that heaven's real miracles will endure turning, being inside and outside both alike — offered as the reason the sign was worth reversing.

34.pericope_label: The Spirit clothes Gideon and the tribes muster

schools.summary: Gill records that the Hebrew says the Spirit clothed Gideon and rules out one construction of the gift: not the spirit of prophecy, whatever Maimonides may say in calling this the first degree of it, but a spirit of fortitude and courage, as the Targum has it. He explains the summons in two stages, the horn reaching the Abiezrites near at hand and messengers carrying the appeal to the rest of Manasseh further off, and rejects the notion that both halves of the tribe are meant.
Clarke says the least and the same: Gideon was endued with preternatural courage and wisdom.

Ellicott collects the other men the figure is used of, Othniel and Jephthah and Samson, and follows it into the New Testament where the disciples are to be clothed with power and believers have put on Christ; he identifies the horn as the shophar and reads the blast as the start of a second obedience, the first call having been answered at Ophrah. Reading the roll of tribes, he notes that Asher partly redeemed a reputation tarnished by an earlier defection and did not linger this time among the sands of Accho or the rocks of the Tyrian Ladder, that Zebulun and Naphtali distinguished themselves as in the campaign against Jabin, that Issachar bowed his shoulder to the yoke as before — perhaps because holding the battle-field of Palestine was bad for a tribe's independence — and that Ephraim, fierce and jealous of any leader not of their own blood, was not asked at all. Keil and Delitzsch press the figure hard: the Spirit descended and laid itself about him like a coat of mail, so that in its strength he was neither to be wounded nor beaten, and the trumpet then summoned Israel to battle.

36.pericope_label: The fleece wet and the floor dry

schools.summary: Gill settles whom Gideon addressed — not, as Ben Gersom held, a prophet standing by, but God in prayer, which is Abarbinel's view — locates the experiment on the threshing-floor where he had been working and the angel had first appeared, open to the sky so that dew could fall freely, and takes the miracle as granted for the confirming of his faith and the encouragement of the men with him.

Clarke calls Gideon very bold and God very condescending and suspects the request itself was prompted by the Spirit; then he gives most of his space to Origen's eighth homily and reproduces the scheme entire — the fleece the Jewish nation, wet while all around is dry and then dry while all around is watered, the floor the people of Judea winnowed by the Gospel, the dew wrung into the bowl the doctrine of Christianity drawn out of the Jewish writings and figured when Christ poured water into a basin. His verdict is mixed: some will think it trifling, yet scarcely a pious mind can read the homily without drinking in a measure of the same spirit, and though he does not follow the method himself and cannot recommend it, of dealers in such small wares we have many that imitate Benjamin Keach and few that come nigh to Origen.

Ellicott reads the hesitation as a measure of the crisis rather than a lapse, since Gideon could see that human strength would be useless against so countless a horde; he corrects the painters who make the fleece a whole sheepskin, a mistake he traces to the Vulgate and Luther, and then admits that the first sign might have come about naturally — which is exactly what shows the narrative honest, since Gideon would hardly have asked for a proof he knew to be no proof. Bishop Hervey's citation of Lord Bacon supplies the physics, sailors hanging fleeces over their ships' sides at night and wringing fresh water from them by morning, and he notes that the psalm about rain coming down into a fleece uses the same word, though there the sense may be mown grass. He identifies the vessel by the Hebrew name it shares with the lordly dish of the earlier song. Keil and Delitzsch have Gideon up early, pressing and squeezing the fleece until he had a vessel full of water out of it, so heavily had the dew fallen while the ground round about stayed dry.

outliers: Clarke's treatment is almost wholly Origen's: he prints the whole allegorical scheme of the eighth homily on Judges, praises its sincerity and unction, and then declines to recommend the method.
themes: a sign that might be natural

schools.summary: Gill notes that the second request came on the morning after the first answer and in the same way as before, and remarks only that night is the season when dew falls.

Ellicott observes that the apology repeats Abraham's word for word, and cannot pass the idiom in it: the noun our version renders anger is literally nose, the dilating nostril having made the word for the feature the word for the passion, as it still is across many Eastern tongues. He points out that an outcome running clean against natural circumstance could have come from nothing but direct interposition — and then draws a line against reading more into it. The dew can be allegorised as grace poured on Israel while the world lies dry, or as God manifesting himself in his people's weakness while the nations flourish; St Ambrose found the Hebrew nation hiding the mystery of Christ in the wet fleece and losing it in the dry; the floor might as easily be made a type of the universal Church. Such applications of a plain narrative he calls precarious at best, and thinks even less of Ewald's likening of the fleece to Gideon's own temper, cool amid the general passion. Keil and Delitzsch explain why a second sign was needed at all — the first was not conclusive, wool being apt to draw dew when things beside it stay dry — and defend the asking: it came not from distrust of what God had promised but from the weakness of the flesh, which cramps the strength of the spirit's faith and leaves God's servants downcast until he relieves them with another display of his power. Gideon knew himself, and knew his own strength was not equal to what lay before him.

outliers: Ellicott closes the chapter by refusing the allegorical readings the sign has attracted — including St Ambrose's and Ewald's — as precarious applications of a simple narrative.
themes: let not thine anger be hot
